For mathematical tractability, and trying to bring out the structure of a reasonable baseline in the more general log-concave situation, we still consider weighted empirical means and not weighted MLEs, as required in the selective removal algorithm.. With probability atleast $1-\delta$ , the resulting distribution $p_{\mu}$ satisfies $(f_{d}\leftrightarrow\alpha,f_{c}\leftrightarrow\varepsilon)$ unlearning 2 with $d(n,\delta)=\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\delta)}{2n}}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\alpha\leq\alpha_{M}(S):=\Delta-\varepsilon_{m}(S),\varepsilon\geq\varepsilon_{m}(S):=\frac{n_{1}^{\prime}}{n_{1}^{\prime}+n_{2}}F_{X}^{-1}\left(\frac{n_{1}^{\prime}}{n_{1}}+d(n_{1},\delta)\right)+2\gamma_{X}(n_{2},1,\delta) $$

where $\Delta=|\mu_{1}-\nu_{1}|$ , $n_{1}^{\prime}=n_{1}-n_{r}$ , $\gamma_{X}(n,1,\delta)>0$ is a number dependent on the distribution $p_{0}$ (symmetric log-concave) such that for $n$ samples $X_{1},\cdots,X_{n}$ IID from $p_{0}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{P}\left[|\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}|\geq n\gamma_{X}(n,1,2\delta)\right]\leq\delta\leftrightarrow 2\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\geq n\gamma_{X}(n,1,2\delta)\right]\leq\delta $$

Moreover, $F_{X}^{-1}$ is the functional inverse3939 39 Similar to the Gaussian $F_{1}^{-1}$ for any symmetric log-concave noise $p_{0}$ with a Lebesgue density, $F_{X}^{-1}$ exists. of the CDF $F_{X}:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to[0,1)$ defined as

$$ F_{X}(t):=\mathbb{P}[|X+\mu_{1}-\nu_{1}|_{2}\leq t]\text{ with }X\sim p_{0}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is the same as that of the finite sample Gaussian result 6, since from 10, we are in search of $(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ pairs so that $T(p,p_{1})\leq f_{d}\leftrightarrow|\mu_{1}-\mu|_{2}\geq\alpha$ and $T(p,q_{1})\geq f_{c}\leftrightarrow|\nu_{1}-\mu|_{2}\leq\varepsilon$ . Similarly, if $\alpha>\Delta+\varepsilon$ , then the feasible region is itself empty 10. Now, we recall that

$$ p_{1}\overset{d}{=}\mu_{1}+X,q_{1}\overset{d}{=}\nu_{1}+X\in\mathcal{P}=\{p_{\mu}\overset{d}{=}\mu+X:\mu\in\mathbb{R}\}. $$

From our assumption, we are given $n_{1}$ IID samples $x_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{1}^{(n_{1})}$ from $p_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ IID samples $x_{2}^{(1)},\ldots,x_{2}^{(n_{2})}$ from $q_{1}$ . Let $\Delta:=|\nu_{1}-\mu_{1}|$ . The distance-based selection removal algorithm 4.2 removes $n_{r}\leq n_{1}$ selected samples from the unwanted distribution $p_{1}$ with the $n_{r}$ largest distances to $\hat{\nu}_{1}\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{n_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{2}}x_{2}^{(i)}$ the empirical estimator of the mean of $q_{1}$ . We denote by $x_{1}^{(1:n_{1})},\ldots,x_{1}^{(n_{1}:n_{1})}$ the original $n_{1}$ samples from $p_{1}$ reordered by increasing distance to $\hat{\nu}_{1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle||x_{1}^{(1:n_{1})}-\hat{\nu}_{1}||_{2}\leq\ldots\leq||x_{1}^{(n_{1}:n_{1})}-\hat{\nu}_{1}||_{2}, $$

with ties broken arbitrarily, then distance-based selection retains only $x_{1}^{(1:n_{1})},\ldots,x_{1}^{(n_{1}^{\prime}:n_{1})}$ to obtain

$$ \hat{\mu}_{1}^{\prime}\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{n_{1}^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}^{\prime}}x_{1}^{(i:n_{1})}. $$

Subsequently, we set the center $\mu$ of the unlearned distribution $p$ to be the following weighted mean.

$$ \mu=\frac{n_{1}^{\prime}\hat{\mu}_{1}^{\prime}+n_{2}\hat{\nu}_{1}}{n_{1}^{\prime}+n_{2}}, $$

where $\hat{\mu}_{1}=\tfrac{1}{n_{1}^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}^{\prime}}x_{1}^{(i:n_{1})}$ and $\hat{\nu}_{1}=\tfrac{1}{n_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{2}}x_{2}^{(i)}$ are the empirical mean estimators.

$$ \mu=\frac{n_{1}^{\prime}\hat{\mu}_{1}^{\prime}+n_{2}\hat{\nu}_{1}}{n_{1}^{\prime}+n_{2}},\text{ where }\hat{\mu}_{1}^{\prime}:=\tfrac{1}{n_{1}^{\prime}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}^{\prime}}x_{1}^{(i)}\text{ and }\hat{\nu}_{1}:=\tfrac{1}{n_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{2}}x_{2}^{(i)}. $$

From the assumption on the quantity $\gamma_{X}(n,1,\delta)$ analogous to the Laurent-Massart bound 37, and from the definition of the quantity $F_{X}$ , using the corresponding Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality 44, we have the following with probability at least $1-\delta$ , using the union bound

$$ \displaystyle|\hat{\mu}_{1}^{\prime}-\nu_{1}|\leq F_{X}^{-1}\left(\frac{n_{1}^{\prime}}{n_{1}}+d(n_{1},\delta)\right)+2\gamma_{X}(n_{2},1,\delta),\quad|\hat{\nu}_{1}-\nu_{1}|\leq\gamma_{X}(n_{2},1,\delta) $$

Now, one can repeat the arguments of the Preservation and the Removal bounds 14 to conclude. ∎

#### Remark 49 (Benefits of Selective removal over Random removal).

We observe that in a one-dimensional shifted Gaussian family, a sufficient condition for the superior behavior of the Selective removal over the random removal requires us to be in the regime of removing at least more than half the unwanted samples.
